vjimc-2004-cat1-01.title: Mean value theorem and Darboux-type continuity
vjimc-2004-cat1-01.body:
Let $b\in[0,1]$ be a point where $f$ attains its maximum. Then $f(b)\ge f(a)=\sqrt3>0$, so $b\in(0,1)$ and $f'(b)=0$.

**A tangent of slope $\sqrt3$.** By the mean value theorem there is $x_0\in(0,b)$ with $f'(x_0)=\frac{f(b)-f(0)}{b}\ge\frac{\sqrt3}{b}>\sqrt3$ (as $b<1$). Since $f'$ is continuous with $f'(x_0)>\sqrt3>0=f'(b)$, the set $\{x\in[x_0,b]: f'(x)=\sqrt3\}$ is non-empty and closed; let $y_1$ be its largest element. Then $y_1<b$ and $f'(x)<\sqrt3$ on $(y_1,b]$ (otherwise the intermediate value theorem would give a larger point with $f'=\sqrt3$). By the mean value theorem $f(b)-f(y_1)<\sqrt3(b-y_1)$, hence
$$f(y_1)>f(b)-\sqrt3(b-y_1)\ge\sqrt3(1-b+y_1)>0 .$$

**A tangent of slope $-\sqrt3$.** Symmetrically, there is $x_1\in(b,1)$ with $f'(x_1)=\frac{f(1)-f(b)}{1-b}\le-\frac{\sqrt3}{1-b}<-\sqrt3$; let $y_2$ be the smallest point of $[b,x_1]$ with $f'(y_2)=-\sqrt3$. Then $f'>-\sqrt3$ on $[b,y_2)$ and, as above, $f(y_2)>f(b)-\sqrt3(y_2-b)\ge \sqrt3(1-y_2+b)>0$.

**The triangle.** The tangent $t_1$ at $y_1$ has slope $\sqrt3$ (inclination $60^\circ$) and meets the $x$-axis at $p_1=y_1-f(y_1)/\sqrt3<y_1$. The tangent $t_2$ at $y_2$ has slope $-\sqrt3$ (inclination $120^\circ$) and meets the $x$-axis at $p_2=y_2+f(y_2)/\sqrt3>y_2$. Since $y_1<b<y_2$, we have $p_1<p_2$. The lines through $(p_1,0)$ and $(p_2,0)$ with these inclinations meet above the segment $[p_1,p_2]$, and the triangle they form with this segment has base angles $60^\circ$ and $60^\circ$; hence it is equilateral. ∎

vjimc-2004-cat1-02.title: Telescoping arctangents
vjimc-2004-cat1-02.body:
For $u,v\ge 0$ the angles $\arctan u,\arctan v$ lie in $[0,\pi/2)$, so $\arctan u-\arctan v\in(-\pi/2,\pi/2)$ and taking tangents gives
$$\arctan u-\arctan v=\arctan\frac{u-v}{1+uv}.$$
With $u=n+1$, $v=n$ (note $1+n(n+1)=1+n+n^2$):
$$\arctan\frac{1}{1+n+n^2}=\arctan(n+1)-\arctan n .$$
Hence the partial sums telescope:
$$\sum_{n=0}^{N}\arctan\frac{1}{1+n+n^2}=\arctan(N+1)-\arctan 0\xrightarrow[N\to\infty]{}\frac\pi2 .$$
**Answer: $\dfrac{\pi}{2}$.**

vjimc-2004-cat1-02.title: Arguments of complex numbers
vjimc-2004-cat1-02.body:
$\arctan\frac{1}{1+n+n^2}$ is the argument of $z_n=(1+n+n^2)+i$. Now
$$\big(1+(n+1)i\big)\big(1-ni\big)=1+n(n+1)+i\big((n+1)-n\big)=(1+n+n^2)+i ,$$
so $\arg z_n=\arg(1+(n+1)i)-\arg(1+ni)=\arctan(n+1)-\arctan n$ (all arguments taken in $(-\pi/2,\pi/2)$, where they add without wrapping). Summing from $n=0$ to $N$ gives $\arctan(N+1)\to\pi/2$.

**Answer: $\dfrac{\pi}{2}$.**

vjimc-2004-cat1-03.title: Pack blocks of disks into shrinking squares
vjimc-2004-cat1-03.body:
**Yes.** Although $\sum 1/n$ diverges, the total *area* $\sum\pi/n^2$ is finite, and we can pack the disks into squares that shrink to a point.

For $k=0,1,2,\dots$ let $Q_k$ be the closed square $[s_k,s_k+2^{2-k}]\times[0,2^{2-k}]$ where $s_k=\sum_{j<k}2^{2-j}$. So the squares have sides $4,2,1,\frac12,\dots$, they are placed side by side along the $x$-axis, their interiors are pairwise disjoint, and $s_k\to 8$.

Put the disks with radii $\frac1n$, $4^k\le n<4^{k+1}$ (that is $3\cdot4^k$ disks) into $Q_k$: divide $Q_k$ into a $2^{k+1}\times2^{k+1}$ grid of $4^{k+1}$ small closed squares of side $2^{2-k}/2^{k+1}=2^{1-2k}$. There are enough small squares ($3\cdot 4^k\le 4^{k+1}$), so assign different small squares to different $n$ and let $z_n$ be the centre of the small square assigned to $n$. Since the radius $\frac1n\le 4^{-k}$ is at most half the side $2^{1-2k}$, the open disk $B(z_n,\frac1n)$ lies in the interior of its small square. (For $k=0$: radii $1,\frac12,\frac13$ in three of the four $2\times2$ quarters of the $4\times4$ square; for $k=1$: radii $\frac14,\dots,\frac1{15}$ in the sixteen $\frac12\times\frac12$ cells of the $2\times2$ square, etc.)

**Disjointness.** Different small squares (in the same or in different $Q_k$) have disjoint interiors, so the disks are pairwise disjoint.

**Convergence.** For $4^k\le n<4^{k+1}$ the point $z_n$ lies in $Q_k$, so
$$|z_n-(8,0)|\le (8-s_k)+\operatorname{diam}Q_k=2^{3-k}+\sqrt2\,2^{2-k}\xrightarrow[k\to\infty]{}0 .$$
Hence $z_n\to(8,0)$. ∎

**Answer: Yes.**

vjimc-2004-cat1-03.title: Columns of disks along a convergent series
vjimc-2004-cat1-03.body:
Another explicit construction (from the official solutions). Group the indices into "columns" $m^2\le n<(m+1)^2$, $m\ge1$, and put
$$z_n=(x_n,y_n),\qquad x_n=\sum_{i=1}^{m}\frac{6}{i^2},\qquad y_n=\sum_{i=m^2}^{n}\frac{3}{i}\qquad(m=\lfloor\sqrt n\rfloor).$$

* *Convergence:* $x_n\to\sum_{i\ge1}6/i^2=\pi^2$, and $0\le y_n\le \sum_{i=m^2}^{m^2+2m}\frac3i\le\frac{3(2m+1)}{m^2}\to0$, so $z_n\to(\pi^2,0)$.
* *Same column:* consecutive centres $z_n,z_{n+1}$ in a column satisfy $y_{n+1}-y_n=\frac{3}{n+1}\ge\frac1n+\frac1{n+1}$ (since $\frac{2}{n+1}\ge\frac1n$ for $n\ge1$), and $y$ increases along the column, so any two disks of the same column are disjoint.
* *Different columns:* every disk of column $m$ has radius $\le\frac1{m^2}$, so it lies in the strip $|x-X_m|<\frac1{m^2}$ with $X_m=\sum_{i\le m}6/i^2$. Since $X_{m+1}-X_m=\frac{6}{(m+1)^2}>\frac1{m^2}+\frac1{(m+1)^2}$ (true because $5m^2>(m+1)^2$ for $m\ge1$), these strips are pairwise disjoint.

So the disks are pairwise disjoint and the centres converge. **Answer: Yes.**

vjimc-2004-cat1-04.title: Factor $y^2-1$ with $y=\frac{n-m}2$
vjimc-2004-cat1-04.body:
**These pairs work:** $1+(2^t-1)=2^t$ and $1\cdot(2^t-1)+1=2^t$; $(2^t-1)+(2^t+1)=2^{t+1}$ and $(2^t-1)(2^t+1)+1=4^t$.

**No others.** Let $m+n=2^k$ and $mn+1=2^l$ with $m,n\ge1$. Then $2^l\ge 2$, so $mn+1$ is even and $m,n$ are both odd. Note also
$$2^l-2^k=(mn+1)-(m+n)=(m-1)(n-1)\ge 0 .\tag{1}$$

*Case $m=n$.* Then $m=2^{k-1}$ is odd, so $m=n=1$, which is in the list ($t=1$).

*Case $m<n$* (the case $m>n$ is symmetric). Put $y=\frac{n-m}2$, a positive integer. Then
$$y^2-1=\Big(\frac{n+m}{2}\Big)^2-mn-1=4^{k-1}-2^l .$$

* If $y=1$: $n=m+2$ and $m+n=2^k$ give $m=2^{k-1}-1$, $n=2^{k-1}+1$ with $k\ge2$ — in the list with $t=k-1$.
* If $y>1$: then $4^{k-1}>2^l$, so $2k-2>l$ and $2^l$ divides $4^{k-1}-2^l=(y-1)(y+1)$. As $l\ge1$, $y$ is odd; $y-1$ and $y+1$ are consecutive even numbers, so one of them is $\equiv2\pmod 4$ and the other must be divisible by $2^{l-1}$. Both are positive, so $y+1\ge 2^{l-1}$, hence $y-1\ge 2^{l-1}-2$ and
$$4^{k-1}-2^l=(y+1)(y-1)\ge 2^{l-1}(2^{l-1}-2)=4^{l-1}-2^l$$
(if $2^{l-1}-2<0$ the right side is negative and the inequality is trivial). Thus $k\ge l$. Combined with (1), $2^l-2^k=(m-1)(n-1)\ge0$ forces $k=l$ and $(m-1)(n-1)=0$, so $m=1$ and $n=2^k-1$ — in the list.

**Answer:** $(1,2^t-1)$, $(2^t-1,1)$, $(2^t-1,2^t+1)$, $(2^t+1,2^t-1)$, $t\ge1$ (e.g. $(1,1),(1,3),(3,5),(7,9),(1,7),\dots$). ∎

vjimc-2004-cat1-04.title: Work modulo powers of 2
vjimc-2004-cat1-04.body:
Write $m+n=2^a$, $mn+1=2^b$. As in (1) above, $2^b-2^a=(m-1)(n-1)\ge0$, so $b\ge a$.

* If $b=a$, then $(m-1)(n-1)=0$: $\{m,n\}=\{1,2^a-1\}$.
* Let $b>a$. If $a=1$, then $m=n=1$, but then $b=a$; so $a\ge2$. If $a=2$, $\{m,n\}=\{1,3\}$ — again $b=a$. So let $a\ge3$. Both $m,n$ are odd, and they cannot both be $\equiv3\pmod 4$ (else $m+n\equiv2\pmod4$), nor both $\equiv1$ (same reason). By symmetry $m=4c+1$, $n=4d+3$. Then
$$(m+1)(n+1)=mn+1+m+n=2^a+2^b=2^a(2^{b-a}+1),$$
while $(m+1)(n+1)=8(2c+1)(d+1)$. As $2c+1$ and $2^{b-a}+1$ are odd, $2^{a-3}\mid d+1$; write $d+1=x\,2^{a-3}$ with $x\ge1$. Then $n=4(d+1)-1=x\,2^{a-1}-1$ and $m=2^a-n=2^a-x2^{a-1}+1\ge1$ gives $x\le 2$.
    * $x=1$: $n=2^{a-1}-1$, $m=2^{a-1}+1$.
    * $x=2$: $n=2^a-1$, $m=1$ (then actually $b=a$).

So $\{m,n\}=\{1,2^a-1\}$ or $\{2^{t}-1,2^{t}+1\}$, and these all work. ∎
